title: Veteran property tax exemption
summary: Vermont exempts $10,000 of appraisal value on the home of a Veteran receiving disability compensation at 50 percent or more. Your town can vote to raise that to as much as $40,000, so the amount depends on where you live.
amount: $10,000 of appraisal value, which a town may vote to increase to up to $40,000
eligibility: The property is your established residence, owned in fee simple by you, your spouse, widow, widower or child, or jointly

One or more of you receives disability compensation for at least 50 percent disability, death compensation, dependence and indemnity compensation, or a pension for disability paid through any military department or the Veterans Administration
Any part of the property used for business or rental is excluded
An unremarried widow or widower of a previously qualified Veteran is entitled to the exemption whether or not they themselves receive government compensation or pension
Only one exemption is allowed per property
details: The town option is the part worth acting on. By majority vote at an annual or special meeting warned for the purpose, a town may increase the exemption to up to $40,000 of appraisal value. Once voted it stays until amended or repealed by a similar vote. If your town has not voted one, that is a thing to raise locally.
Note the 50 percent threshold. Vermont sets the bar lower than many states, which require 70 or 100 percent.

Apply to the Office of Veterans Affairs before 1 May each year, with a written statement from the Military Department or the VA. This is unusual: you file with the state Veterans office rather than your town assessor.
If your disability is permanent you only need to apply once, before 1 May of the first year.
The surviving spouse provision is notably generous. An unremarried widow or widower keeps the exemption even if they receive no compensation or pension of their own.
Both the $10,000 and the $40,000 ceiling are fixed in the statute with no inflation adjustment, so changing them requires legislation, or a town vote within the existing ceiling.
agency: Vermont Office of Veterans Affairs, with the exemption applied by the town

title: Military retirement and survivor benefits, excluded below an income limit
summary: Vermont excludes all federally taxable military retirement and survivor benefit income if your federal adjusted gross income is $125,000 or less. Between $125,000 and $175,000 the exclusion tapers away, and above $175,000 there is none.
amount: Full exclusion at federal AGI of $125,000 or less, tapering to nothing at $175,000
eligibility: You receive US military retirement income, or US military survivor benefit income as an eligible beneficiary
If your federal adjusted gross income is $125,000 or less, all federally taxable military retirement and survivor benefit income is excluded
If it is above $125,000 but below $175,000, a proportional share is excluded
If it is $175,000 or more, nothing is excluded
details: The taper is linear rather than a cliff. The excluded share is 175,000 minus your federal adjusted gross income, divided by 50,000, applied to your federally taxable military retirement and survivor income.
This is not a fixed dollar cap. Below the threshold the whole amount comes out, however large it is, which is more generous than the capped exclusions several neighbouring states use.
A taxpayer eligible for the military exclusion may elect it even while also electing one of Vermont's other retirement income exclusions.
The thresholds are stated as fixed dollar figures with no indexing, so they do not move with inflation.
The current form of this provision took effect on 1 January 2025.
